Now, it's time for reconnaissance. With the dense vegetation, you couldn't see what you were doing. Hopefully some of it has been cleared so you can get in there and see. By the way, the chemical you’re using is similar to a notorious herbicide that was part of a controversial defoliant. I give you permission to play dramatic music while you do this.

Go around the property. You're looking for something: trunks. You want to locate every trunk and stem that's coming out of the ground. Think of it as looking for a hidden nest. Don't cut them, just mark them on the soil with some kind of bright spray paint or something, so you can find them again easily. Don't paint the trunks because that's where the herbicide is going to go, and you don't want to seal off any cells or bark. Spray the ground.

Be aware that many people get a rash from handling certain invasive plants, so cover up for this. Especially watch your face, as the vines will whip around.

Once you have them all marked, you're going to move into Phase 2: The Shreddening (aka "Stem Injection Frilling or Hack-and-Squirt" but I like "The Shreddening" better). You want some undiluted concentrate in a squirt bottle, and some kind of sharp tool with which to shred, score, and otherwise rip up the bark on each and every stem and trunk that comes out of the ground. I use an old serrated pruning saw to scratch the bark all up. A steak knife or old serrated bread knife works. Girdle the stem, too. Pour that good stuff all over the torn bark and cambium, getting it into the cuts.

On vigorous, mature plants, this works better than the cut-stump-and-paint technique, because when you cut the stump, the cells immediately begin to close it off, and there's a very short window of time for the stump to absorb the herbicide. And besides, you're reserving that for Phase 3, should you need it.

Now, if you want to, to spare your collateral damage, you can skip Phase 1 with the hose-end sprayer, and go straight to The Shreddening. However, in my experience, with vines of this size and maturity, it's better if you soften it up first with some spraying, start getting those biochemical processes all messed up. But if the idea of dousing your entire property with herbicide is disturbing, that's fine. It will just take longer this way.

So, you go around and administer weedkiller concentrate to the cuts, making sure to work quickly while the cuts are still fresh, before the cells have a chance to seal them off. Then you wait another couple of weeks.

By this time you should be seeing major dieback, but you need to give it time to finish dying. You won't really know it's dead until summer 2018 (yes, that's not a typo, 2018, two years after the next presidential election) and it hasn't come back.

So when you see new branches coming out of a trunk (and AS SOON AS you see them, not "next weekend" or "pretty soon now" or "when we get back from vacation"), you do Phase 3: The Stumpening. You probably can't do Phase 2 again because it's all shredded to heck.

This is where you cut off the vine, snip it right off with loppers, pruners, or a pruning saw, and paint or squirt concentrate on the cut end of the stump, again, working quickly before the cells can seal it off. If you see some spots where another Shreddening would be productive, go for it.

Cut it off about 12" above the ground. This leaves you room to redo The Stumpening an inch lower down, should you need to in the future.

If, at any time in this process, you see new shoots coming directly out of the ground, you can either spray them with a standard dose of the weedkiller from an ordinary ready-to-use sprayer (like the gallon size you can buy at a local store, no need to get out the hose-end sprayer for a single shoot), or simply snip them off with the pruners. They are evidence of the plant's last stand. It's giving up on the existing top growth and is trying to reboot itself from the roots. Weedkiller will give it an additional dose of poison; snipping it off will simply remove its photosynthesis from the equation.

But whichever, do *something*. Don't be like, Oh, huh, there's another shoot. Get *after* it, snip that off with whatever you have on hand if nothing else.

So, this is your life until summer 2018. Eternal vigilance.

First, the baby parasitic bird doesn't necessarily eliminate the rightful heirs. It out-competes them for food, with the biggest and loudest gaping mouth when the parents arrive with food, but if the baby songbirds are big and strong, they get their fair share and manage to fledge. Before you cover the entire backyard with landscape fabric and wood chips, you would need to have written permission from your landlord, as you would be effectively removing the lawn. 

Currently, the property is "house + lawn," and even if the lawn is technically weeds, legally, "if it's green, it's good," and it is still considered a lawn. 

If you kill whatever "lawn" exists by covering it with weed barrier and mulch (which will kill it in about two months), you change the property from "house + lawn" to "house + wood chips," which is not the same. It's harder to rent a "house + wood chips" than a "house + lawn." People prefer a lawn for their kids and pets to play on and for cookouts, even if it's mostly weeds.

You would need the same permission if you were planning to till it up and plant vegetables or flowers. 

You could consider xeriscaping instead of laying down wood chips (with written permission), but xeriscaping can be expensive. Plants and rocks cost a lot, and a "few hundred dollars" won't go very far.

Nitrogen in snow is primarily relevant for agricultural and landscaping purposes. There's no practical way to utilize it in any other context.

As precipitation falls through the atmosphere, it collects atmospheric nitrogen which is in the NH2 form. When snow accumulates on thawed soil, it slowly melts, allowing a gradual release of NH2 into the soil profile. Conversion to NH3 and nitrate fixing occurs without the microbial inhibiting effects of commercial anhydrous ammonia. Since the ground is already thawed, most of the moisture and nitrogen seep into the soil profile, contributing to the total nitrogen content.

The amount of nitrogen is very small. It's only significant when considered in the context of a farmer managing a large area that will require anhydrous ammonia in the spring. A heavy snow cover during the previous winter can reduce the amount needed for purchase.

A lawn that has had large snow piles on it throughout the winter will often "green up" better in the spring in the areas where the snow piles were.

I suppose you could collect snow, allow it to melt, then store it and use it, but it seems like a lot of extra work for very little reward.

You live in a climate zone where historically, according to data collected for decades by agricultural organizations, your temperature drops to 15F at least once a decade. That is what the climate zones mean--"historically, on average, this is as cold as it gets here once every 10 years." This does not take into consideration the occasional extraordinary weather events. That's your normal baseline climate. Once every 10 years, on average, you can expect it to drop to at least 15F. Those statistics are what define your climate zone.

It doesn't signify what the weather is doing lately, that it "seldom gets below freezing here" *lately*. What does signify is that it has the *potential* to get far, far below freezing. You'd have to live in a much warmer climate before you'd be able to truthfully say, "It seldom gets below freezing here."

So this is why, when you're choosing trees, shrubs, and perennials, you go "one zone colder." If you live in your current zone, you choose trees, shrubs, and perennials that are winter-hardy to the next lower zone, or even lower. You don't choose them based on the fact that *lately* it seldom gets below freezing--you choose them based on what the climate *can* do. This gives you plenty of cushion in that one winter every 10 years when it does get down to 15F, while all around you are neighbors with dead landscaping and container plants that got left out.

General purpose potting soil used straight out of the bag is usually rather dense and slow-draining, so I wonder whether you may have left the original root ball intact and simply filled in around it with the potting soil. Most similar plants are potted in media that contains a high percentage of peat moss, if it's not 100% peat moss. When a root ball of peat dries out completely, it becomes hydrophobic, and water simply runs off it.

This would mean that when you're sticking your finger into the soil to feel it, you're feeling the narrow band of potting soil that runs around the outside of the root ball, which dries out quickly since it's so narrow.

I am temporarily between collections of a specific type of flowering houseplant, after having undergone a lengthy ordeal with pests that eventually required discarding the entire group, and I'm not really over it yet and ready to start over, but before that, I had them since 1975.

The big thing with them is, besides the usual advice about overwatering and "only water when the soil is dry," is that they hate wide swings between wet and dry.

If you let it get so dry that the leaves go limp, and then flood it with water in an agony of apologetic remorse, that's a plant that's 85% likely to come down with root rot. The fine root hairs die in the drought, and then the flooding shuts off all the oxygen between the soil particles, so anaerobic rot bacteria get started, and this type of plant just seems peculiarly susceptible to root rot. Nothing on their fast-draining native hillsides prepared them evolutionarily to cope with excess water at the roots. The fine root hairs are dead, so it can't uptake water and nutrients in order to repair itself and grow more fine root hairs.

So it then frequently becomes a downward death spiral that is very hard to fix. You can cut off the top and try to root it with rooting hormone, but it's best just to not let them get that dry in the first place.

OR, when you discover that you let them dry out to the point of wilting, don't flood them, but instead give them just a tiny wetting of the soil, and then do it again the next day, and so forth, until the potting mix is once again moist.

So this is how they get their reputation for being difficult. They want their soil evenly moist, and by evenly moist, they mean evenly moist, and not "sporadically watered whenever you remember." Even a notably temperamental type of fern is a better sport about being allowed to get too dry and then being rehydrated. It'll shed brown leaflets all over the table, but at least it won't die.

This type of flowering plant can die. Their leaves become mushy, and when you're at the mushy stage, there's no fix. Even trying to salvage a leaf from the unblemished center may not work, as it's not mature enough and doesn't have the reserves to start new growth.

So, they're difficult if you're not the sort of person who can obsessively check a plant's moisture level with a finger every single day. Because a plant can be "mmm, still doesn't need water" on one day and then by the next day need watering today, not tomorrow.

The mass market cultivars are a lot better about tolerating haphazard watering than the cultivars you buy from specialized breeders, but even they have their limits. If you buy a half-dead flowerless garden center survivor in the middle of summer, you'll know that's a potential survivor and is a good bet, but, again, even it will have its limits.

So you keep it evenly moist by doing equal parts of peat moss, vermiculite, and perlite. You'll note that this has no potting soil. In the wild, they live in tiny pockets of leaf mold in the limestone bedrock, so they need a mix that's light, loose, but moisture-retentive. The peat moss and vermiculite do the moisture thing, the perlite adds lightness.

So you need to fertilize regularly, as this is nutrient-free.

Since this is peat moss, once it dries out it's very difficult to rehydrate. So another reason for the daily finger check. You can't let it dry out completely.

So if you can live with something that requires a daily finger check for moisture, you will have no trouble growing this type of flowering plant. If you're the sort who waters other houseplants only when you notice they're wilted, you're going to have a bad time.

There is always wick or capillary watering, but it can take some tinkering to get it right. I did it for a while, and I found that the savings in time and convenience wasn't worth the tradeoff of constant monitoring, as you still have to check it every day to be sure it's working. "Never let a plant sit in water" is advice that is generally applied to the following situation: You have watered the plant from above, the excess has flowed out the bottom drainage hole into the saucer, and the plant is now sitting in it. You need to remove that excess immediately and not allow the plant to sit in it and reabsorb it, for two reasons:

1. The soil has already received the exact amount of water molecules that it needs to wet it down enough for the roots' needs, and more would be too wet.

2. The water, on its way down the soil column, picks up excess dissolved fertilizer and mineral salts, flushing them out, which prevents buildup and potential fine root hair burn. If you allow the plant to sit in this and reabsorb it, you've just added those all back.

Watering from below is a valid way of watering plants, especially tropicals that are frequently potted in a high proportion of peat moss. Once peat moss dries out completely, it shrinks and becomes hydrophobic, with the result that, when you water from above, the water just runs down the side of the shrunken root ball and out the bottom, not even penetrating the soil. This can lead to your plants always being wilty and unhappy.

So watering from below has the effect of allowing dried-out peat moss to slowly wick itself back to optimal moisture levels, and is helpful with things like ferns, figs, and philodendrons. It lets you be sure that the entire root ball, for these plants who hate drying out too much, has become moistened.

The grass species used as turfgrasses in cold-winter climates in certain regions are genetically hard-wired to shut down in summer heat and drought, so reseeding and overseeding of them is pointless in summer. Mulch is never a bad thing unless you're doing it wrong. Volcano mulching is very bad for trees and other plants with stems that rot if you heap up wet organic rotting material against them, and it's detrimental for plants that need more oxygen that the huge layer of mulch is cutting off. So basically, volcano mulch is not a good technique unless you know what you're doing, so I'd advise beginners to avoid it.

Standard mulching practice is to put down the layer of mulch over the entire planting area, not just in a ring around individual plants, leaving bare soil. This is for two reasons:

1. The bare soil gets weeds. 
2. The bare soil evaporates moisture.

Since the purpose of mulching is to stop weeds and reduce evaporation, mulching only a part of the area is like vaccinating only half the children in a classroom.

The optimal width for a planting area is 4 feet. A person can reach about 2 feet into a bed from a kneeling position at the side, so a bed that's 4 feet wide means you can reach the center without needing to step into the bed itself. So 3-foot beds aren't as efficient a use of space as a 4-foot bed, unless you're cramped for room.
